analysis.one_liner: Phases out feeding medically important antibiotics to farm animals for growth promotion and routine disease prevention.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Health Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug makers to prove that antibiotics routinely fed to pigs, cattle, and poultry pose no risk of creating drug-resistant bacteria in people. Producers still using these antibiotics would have had two years to stop or prove safety, with federal payments to help family and small farms cover the cost of switching. An estimated 70 percent of antibiotics sold in the United States go to farm animals for non-medical purposes like growth promotion, and the bill's findings cite federal studies linking that practice to resistant foodborne infections like Salmonella and E. coli.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, who face a growing threat from antibiotic-resistant infections: the bill cites a National Academy of Sciences estimate that resistant bacteria already cost Americans $4-5 billion a year, and a federal task force warning that common infections could become untreatable. Family-owned and small farms would benefit from priority access to federal payments to help cover the cost of reducing antibiotic use, and colleges would get grants to develop and teach alternatives. Consumers were projected to pay little — the National Academy of Sciences estimated ending feed additives would cost each American less than $5-10 per year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who might ever need an antibiotic

how_it_helps.text: Bars approval of any new animal drug containing antibiotics used in human medicine unless the manufacturer proves a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from resistance, and orders withdrawal of existing approvals for nontherapeutic (growth-promotion and routine prevention) uses within two years unless safety is demonstrated [S2][S3].

Prioritizes family-owned and small farms for federal payments to defray the cost of cutting antibiotic use, easing the transition for the smallest producers rather than leaving them to absorb it [S2][S3].

Requires manufacturers to report and publish annual sales data on these drugs by animal species and purpose, giving the public and regulators visibility into how much antibiotic is going into the food supply [S2][S3].

The bill's findings note the European Union banned feeding medically important antibiotics to healthy animals in 1999 with no significant impact on animal health, food safety, or meat prices, and with resistant bacteria levels declining sharply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of animal antibiotics, which could lose the large nontherapeutic feed-additive market for human-use drugs, and large-scale livestock and poultry operations whose production model relies on routine antibiotics to speed growth and compensate for crowded conditions. Taxpayers would fund the transition payments and research grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Animal drug makers and big livestock operations

drawbacks.text: Livestock producers would face real transition costs: the bill's own findings describe nontherapeutic antibiotics as compensating for crowded, unsanitary, and stressful farming conditions, so operations built around routine antibiotic use would need to change husbandry practices or absorb losses [S3].

The two-year withdrawal deadline is aggressive, and critics of similar proposals argued the science linking low-dose farm use to human infections, while supported by the studies the bill cites, is contested and that an automatic deadline could disrupt meat supply before safety reviews finish [S3].
The bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' in appropriations for producer payments and research grants without a cost ceiling, leaving the taxpayer price tag open-ended [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside is large and long-term — preserving the effectiveness of antibiotics that modern medicine depends on — while the estimated consumer cost is small (under $5-10 per person per year, per the National Academy of Sciences estimate cited in the bill). The real burden falls on a narrow set of manufacturers and large producers, and the bill deliberately cushions small and family farms with payments. The main honest criticism is the speed: a hard two-year deadline applied across whole chemical classes is a blunt instrument, and Congress chose not to test whether a slower FDA-led review could achieve the same result.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Olympia Snowe introduced the bill on April 7, 2005, with Senators Kennedy, Collins, Landrieu, and Reed as original cosponsors [S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The only further action was Snowe's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record on April 11, 2005 [S5].
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no House companion action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of animal antibiotics and large livestock and poultry operations that depend on routine, nonprescription antibiotic use are better off, because nothing forced them to prove the safety of or phase out nontherapeutic feed uses. Antibiotic-resistant infections continued to develop, a cost spread across everyone who may someday need an antibiotic.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Animal drug makers and large livestock producers

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered its introductory remarks in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Kennedy, Collins, Landrieu, and Reed
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan support from both parties.

for.name: More than 300 health, consumer, agricultural, environmental, and humane organizations
for.role: Supporting coalition, including the American Medical Association and American Public Health Association
for.what_they_did: Backed enactment of legislation phasing out nontherapeutic antibiotic use in farm animals, as recited in the bill's own findings.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee, chaired by Sen. Mike Enzi
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; controls whether it gets a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Livestock industry and animal drug manufacturers
against.role: Industries whose sales and production practices the bill would restrict
against.what_they_did: Opposed phasing out routine antibiotic use in farm animals, the position that made the bill politically difficult to advance; opposition from agricultural and animal-health trade groups to this legislation was widely reported at the time.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five Senate sponsors split 3-2 between Democrats and Republicans, and it drew no recorded opposition votes because it never reached the floor; the outcome turned on committee inaction rather than a partisan roll call.

industries.note: The bill would force makers of penicillins, tetracyclines, macrolides, and other human-use antibiotics to prove their farm-feed products pose no resistance risk within two years or lose approval for nontherapeutic use. Most of these products were approved before the FDA considered resistance, so their sales rested on approvals never tested against the modern safety standard the bill would impose.

About 70 percent of U.S. antibiotics go to farm animals for growth promotion and to offset crowded conditions, per the bill's findings. Ending that practice raises production costs for operations built on routine antibiotics, which is why the industry opposed the bill even though the same practice creates the resistant bacteria that endanger consumers.

The bill gives family and small farms priority for federal payments to cover the cost of reducing antibiotic use, plus research grants to demonstrate alternatives — support large operations are less likely to need.
